title: Can Dogs Eat Thanksgiving Turkey?
summary: Can dogs eat Thanksgiving turkey? Learn which parts are safe, which sides to share or skip, and what to do if your dog eats something they shouldn't.

The short answer: yes, dogs can eat turkey breast in small quantities, as it is a lean meat. But, and this is a big BUT, only if there is no skin, no seasoning, and absolutely no bones.


**Content:**


1. Turkey Skin, Bones, Necks and Giblets: What to Skip
2. Leftovers and Other Kinds of Turkey
3. Thanksgiving Sides: Safe vs. Not Safe
4. How to Build a Dog-Friendly Thanksgiving Plate
5. What About Cats?
6. My Dog Ate Something They Shouldn't Have: What Now?
7. Conclusion


## Turkey Skin, Bones, Necks and Giblets: What to Skip


Turkey skin is fatty, and even a small amount can cause a[digestive upset](https://petcube.com/blog/is-your-dogs-stomach-making-noises/) in your pet and can lead to[pancreatitis](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jsap.12293?ref=petcube.com) . Cooked bones, especially poultry bones, splinter when chewed and can cause severe damage to your dog’s or cat’s mouth and digestive tract if eaten. Even if your dog chews bones into fine pieces, those bones can cause[blockages in the intestine](https://petcube.com/blog/swollen-dog-belly/) . Giblets such as livers and kidneys are rich and high in fat, so they shouldn’t be given to your pets if you want to avoid a visit to your local vet. Raw meat and bones carry the risk of[salmonella](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0362028X23050019?ref=petcube.com) , so they should always be avoided by humans and pets alike.


Dr. Mansfield says:


> “[Acute pancreatitis](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/veterinary-science-and-veterinary-medicine/acute-pancreatitis?ref=petcube.com) in[dogs](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/veterinary-science-and-veterinary-medicine/dog?ref=petcube.com) is a potentially reversible condition, but in severe forms it can cause systemic and local complications.”


## Leftovers and Other Kinds of Turkey


Generally, plain, boneless, and skinless white turkey meat is safe for your dog in small quantities. Deli meats such as sausage, smoked ham, and other ground meats should be kept out of your dog’s reach. These rich and often fatty meats can easily lead to sore stomachs and pancreatitis. Many foods that are perfectly safe and healthy for people are unsafe and even harmful to pets. These include grapes, onions, and raisins.


## Thanksgiving Sides: Safe vs. Not Safe


There are a few[traditional Thanksgiving sides](https://petcube.com/blog/thanksgiving-foods-your-pet-can-eat/) that can be prepared separately (without any garnishes or seasonings) and safely enjoyed by your pooch.


**The safe list:**


- Plain sweet potatoes (sweet potatoes are packed with vitamins and fiber and make a healthy snack when cooked without spices or seasonings)
- Steamed or raw[green beans](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-vegetables/)
- Pumpkin with no spice
- Fresh cranberries
- Cooked corn off the cob (the cob can be swallowed whole and cause an obstruction)
- Raw or plain cooked carrots
- Potatoes cooked with no salt or seasoning
- Apple slices without the core and seeds


**The unsafe list:**


- Onions
- Garlic
- Gravy and sauces (generally too much salt and fat)
- Turkey stuffing
- Salad dressings
- Any meat or poultry fat
- Smoked meats
- Deli meats and sausages
- Apple cores and seeds (the seeds contain cyanide, and the core can be a[choking](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-choking/) risk)
- Xylitol
- [Chocolate](https://www.aspcapro.org/sites/default/files/m-toxbrief_0201.pdf?ref=petcube.com)
- Mac and cheese (high in fat)
- Desserts and sweets


Pumpkin pie is a fall and winter favorite, but it’s best to save it for the humans and make something separate for your furry friend. Cooked pumpkin (boiled, steamed, or roasted) on its own, with no sugar or spices, is safe for dogs in small amounts. It is very important to remember during this season that xylitol (an artificial sweetener) and chocolate are poisonous to dogs and can cause much more than a digestive upset. If your dog has eaten anything containing xylitol or chocolate, rush them to your closest vet.


Dr. Murphy said in her[article](https://www.vetsmall.theclinics.com/article/S0195-5616(11)00219-1/abstract?ref=petcube.com) *Xylitol Toxicosis in Dogs* :


> “While xylitol is considered safe in humans, canine ingestions have resulted in severe and life-threatening signs associated with increased insulin secretion leading to hypoglycaemia. Acute death due to severe hypoglycaemia if untreated is possible, and liver failure may develop 1 to 3 days after xylitol ingestion.”


## How to Build a Dog-Friendly Thanksgiving Plate


If you want your pooch to enjoy Thanksgiving with you, the safest treat is a tin or pouch of wet food that you can buy at your local vet. If you’d rather make your own feast for your furry friend, use the safe list above to choose which foods to spoil your dog with.


If you’re treating your dog, reduce their meal size and keep[treats](https://petcube.com/blog/healthy-treats/) under 10% of their daily calorie needs. Make sure your guests know not to feed your dog any human food other than what’s on the ‘dog-safe’ plate you’ve prepared.


## What About Cats?


You may be wondering what you can give your cat as a Thanksgiving treat. In short, the same rules apply: plain turkey with no skin, fat, or seasoning is safe to give as a treat in a very small amount.


## My Dog Ate Something They Shouldn't Have: What Now?


If you see or suspect that your dog has eaten something they shouldn’t have, keep a close eye on them for any of the following symptoms:


- [Vomiting](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-vomiting/)
- [Diarrhea](https://petcube.com/blog/diarrhea-in-dogs/)
- Allergic reaction ([swelling](https://petcube.com/blog/dogs-eye-suddenly-swollen/) of the face, muzzle, or around the eyes)
- [Lethargy](https://petcube.com/blog/lethargy-in-dogs/)
- [Bloating](https://petcube.com/blog/dog-bloating/) of the stomach


Many veterinary clinics close over the holidays and on Thanksgiving. Save the contact details of your closest emergency vet on your phone so you know who to call in case of an emergency.


Be sure to dispose of any bones and meat-smelling waste in a secured trash bag, in a closed container, or somewhere completely out of your pet’s reach. While you’re busy hosting, a[Petcube Cam](https://petcube.com/cam/?ref=petcube.com) in the kitchen lets you keep an eye on counter-surfing and trash raids, and the[Petcube App](https://petcube.com/mobile-app/?ref=petcube.com) helps you track any changes in your dog’s symptoms or behavior afterward. If your dog has eaten chocolate or xylitol, don’t wait: take them to your closest emergency vet immediately.


## Conclusion


If you want to treat your dog to a homemade Thanksgiving feast, stick to a few vegetables from the safe list (plain cooked pumpkin, sweet potato, and carrots) and plain turkey without any seasoning or fat.
